messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 64

James is a fifty-five-year-old man, a fact that still surprises him when he catches his reflection in the polished chrome of a kitchen faucet. He has been married to Amina for thirty-two years, and they have three grown children who live in different cities. He retired from the military six years ago, after twenty-eight years of service, and now works as a bomb disposal technician for a private security firm. The work is delicate, precise, and quiet. He likes that about it. He likes the stillness that descends on a site when everyone else has been cleared away, and it is just him and the device. He likes the way his hands do not shake.

He did not grow up near the coast. He grew up in a dry, dusty town in the interior, where the sky was a hard blue and the earth was cracked and red. He joined the military young, and he learned to read explosives the way other men learn to read maps. He learned the language of wires and timers, of pressure plates and mercury switches. He learned that a bomb is a story someone has told, and his job is to understand the ending before it happens. This skill served him well in the army, and it serves him now.

The event that changed everything did not happen in a war zone. It happened on a Tuesday, during a holiday. He and Amina had saved for two years to take a trip to a small island nation, a place with white sand and turquoise water. They had been there for four days. On the fifth day, the water went away. He remembers standing on the beach, watching the ocean pull back, revealing a mile of wet, glistening seabed. He remembers the fish flopping in the shallows. He remembers the strange, low sound, like a train coming from under the earth. He remembers Amina grabbing his arm, and he remembers running. He remembers the wall of water that rose up and ate the sky.

He did not think about his training. He did not think about wires or timers or pressure plates. He thought about nothing. He held onto Amina, and the water took them. He remembers the violence of it, the way the world became a washing machine of debris and sand and salt. He remembers being tumbled, his lungs burning, his shoulder dislocating with a pop he could feel more than hear. He remembers the moment he lost her hand.

He found her three hours later, alive, tangled in the branches of a palm tree that had been bent nearly flat to the ground. She had a deep gash on her leg and a look in her eyes he had never seen before. He carried her for two miles through the mud and the wreckage, stepping over things he did not want to look at. He did not cry. He did not panic. He just moved.

Now, six years later, he cannot stop moving. He cannot sit still. When he is at home, he paces. He checks the locks on the doors three times before bed. He checks the gas stove. He checks the windows. He tells himself it is just good practice, the habit of a careful man. But he knows it is not true. He knows he is waiting for the water to come back.

At work, he is fine. The bomb is a problem he can solve. The wires are a language he speaks fluently. But when he is driving home, and the road curves, and he cannot see what is ahead, his heart begins to pound. He feels the pressure in his chest, the tightness in his throat. He pulls over and waits for it to pass. He does not tell Amina about this. She has her own nightmares now, her own silences.

He has not slept through the night in six years. He wakes at 3:47 AM, every single time, with the sound of that low, earth-shaking groan in his ears. He lies in the dark, his wife breathing beside him, and he listens. He listens for the water. He knows it is irrational. He knows he lives in a landlocked city, in a house on a hill. But the part of him that knows this is a very small part, and it is very quiet. The rest of him is still on that beach, still running, still holding on.
